hadean-eon.text: The eon is named after Hades, the Greek underworld, for hellish conditions: a newly accreted planet whose surface was probably molten.
Hadean rocks are very rare; almost all that survives is zircon grains, mostly from the Jack Hills of Western Australia.
Other records of Hadean time come from the Moon and from meteorites.
Heavy bombardment dominated the eon, and impacts periodically disrupted the ocean.
A thick early atmosphere gave way to a superocean that covered nearly the whole planet.
Land was scarce: continents may have risen in the mid-Hadean and then drowned, which matters for the origin of life.
The mantle churned vigorously, but whether plates moved or a rigid lid covered Earth is still debated.
With oceans in place, life was possible but vulnerable to large impacts.

archean-eon.text: Earth was mostly a water world: continental crust existed, but much of it lay beneath a superocean deeper than today's oceans.
The atmosphere almost entirely lacked free oxygen, holding less than 0.001% of today's level.
The Sun gave only about 75–80% of its present light, yet surface temperatures were near modern levels: the faint young Sun paradox.
More greenhouse gas, including nitrous oxide from abiotic denitrification, or a darker Earth with less land and cloud may explain the warmth.
Earth's heat flow was nearly three times today's when the eon began and still twice today's at its end.
The ocean was broadly reducing, poor in sulfate, and lacked a lasting boundary between oxygenated and oxygen-free water.
Life stayed simple: prokaryotes, both archaea and bacteria, living largely in shallow-water microbial mats and stromatolites.
The first cratons, old and stable blocks of continental lithosphere, formed during this eon.

eoarchean-era.text: The era opens with the Acasta Gneiss of Canada, dated to 4,031 Ma, the oldest preserved rock formation.
Earth had cooled significantly by the start of the Archean, and oceans already covered much of the planet.
Heavy asteroid bombardment marked its beginning, and impacts periodically disrupted the oceans.
Oxygen isotopes show the water cycle was already running in the early Eoarchean.
The earliest record of weathering and the oldest water-laid sediments date to about 3.8 Ga.
The Sun shone at about 70% of its modern brightness, yet liquid water existed.
Continental crust formed at a growing pace, and anaerobic microbes, including early photosynthesisers, appeared from about 3.7 Ga.

paleoarchean-era.text: The Paleoarchean rock record is very limited, and deformation and metamorphism have wiped most of it clean.
Much continental crust existed but was still underwater; it is unclear whether any land stood exposed.
A hotter mantle and a steeper ocean-floor heat gradient ruled out plate tectonics in its modern form.
Cratons grew by accreting terranes; the Kaapvaal and Pilbara cratons formed at the start of the era.
By about 3.4 Ga nitrogen made up most of a stable 'second atmosphere'.
Microbial mats and biofilms became common in shallow water, and anaerobic microbes lived around hot vents and inside buried sediments.
Asteroid impacts were frequent in the early Archean.

mesoarchean-era.text: The Mesoarchean holds the first evidence of modern-style subduction and an expansion of microbial life.
Cratons had low relief and broad shallow seas, and weathering fed nutrients into the oceans.
Microbes with diverse metabolisms spread and released gases that changed the atmosphere's makeup.
Atmospheric nitrogen was probably close to today's level.
The climate was warm or temperate thanks to methane and carbon dioxide, yet the era saw the oldest known glaciation.
Oases of relatively high oxygen formed in some nearshore shallow seas.
A supercontinent, Vaalbara, may have existed.

neoarchean-era.text: Plate tectonics may have resembled today's, though sinking slabs broke off more often in the hotter mantle.
Changing air and soils pushed microbial metabolisms to diversify; more copper in the environment favoured organisms that use oxygen.
Phosphorus from magmatic rocks, organic burial and more oxidized volcanic gases helped build up oxygen, leading toward the Great Oxidation.
Raindrop prints in 2.7 Ga volcanic ash show the air was less than twice as dense as today's.
Gas bubbles in lavas of the same age suggest a pressure near 0.23 bar, at odds with very high carbon dioxide or nitrogen.
The geomagnetic field was closer to a simple dipole than after the era.
Much of the mantle lithosphere beneath today's continents may have formed in this era.

proterozoic-eon.text: The Proterozoic, the longest eon, ran from 2500 to 538.8 Ma; its rock record is far more complete than the Archean's.
About 43% of today's continental crust formed in the Proterozoic, against 39% in the Archean and 18% since.
At the eon's start Earth's internal heat flow was still about twice today's.
The Sun shone 5–18% more weakly than it does now.
Subduction reached levels the Archean, which lacks eclogites, never did.
Sulfidic, oxygen-free (euxinic) waters, rare in the Archean, became more common.
Plankton mass reached roughly modern levels early in the eon.
Its headline events are the Great Oxidation and Huronian glaciation, the first eukaryotes, Snowball Earth and the Ediacaran biota.

paleoproterozoic-era.text: The first and longest era of Earth history, 2500–1600 Ma, split into the Siderian, Rhyacian, Orosirian and Statherian.
The continents first stabilized during this era.
Cyanobacteria are credited with raising atmospheric oxygen from almost none to as much as 10% of today's level.
Ultra-high-temperature metamorphic rocks of this era are taken to mark the start of modern-style tectonics.
Around 1.8 Ga a day lasted about 20 hours, giving roughly 450 days a year.

siderian-period.text: The first Proterozoic period, 2500–2300 Ma, is named from the Greek for iron, after its banded iron formations.
Earth spun faster than today: the day had lengthened to about 21 hours by 2.4 Ga.
Continental plates grew in the early Siderian, and dike swarms cut cratons in North America, South Africa and Australia.
From the period's start, oxygen rose irreversibly in the atmosphere.
As oxygen destroyed methane, from 300 to 4 ppmv, Earth slid into the Huronian glaciation from the mid-Siderian.
Weathering in air raised the sulfur isotope ratio of seawater sulfate, which settled out as gypsum and anhydrite.
Microfossils in Australian black chert and bacterial remains in South African iron formation record the period's life.
Siberia and the Canadian Shield were joined in a continent called Arctica.

rhyacian-period.text: Spanning 2300–2050 Ma, the period takes its name from the Greek for lava flow, for the lava that flowed.
The Huronian glaciation lasted through about the first 40% of the period.
A massive rise in oxygen, expanding life and organic burial drove the Lomagundi carbon isotope excursion; the first red beds formed.
The Bushveld Igneous Complex and similar intrusions formed.
Orogenies in South America and West Africa began building the supercontinent Columbia.
Eukaryotes and sexual reproduction are thought to have originated in this period.
Possible signs of macroscopic life in 2.1 Ga rocks are heavily disputed.

orosirian-period.text: Spanning 2050–1800 Ma, the period is named from the Greek for mountain range, after intense orogeny on virtually all continents in its later half.
Two of Earth's largest known impacts struck: Vredefort early in the period and Sudbury near its end.
Global collisions from 2.1 to 1.8 Ga, such as the Trans-Hudson, Limpopo, Capricorn and Trans-North China orogenies, assembled the supercontinent Columbia.
Atmospheric oxygen fell as increased volcanism released carbon dioxide.
Banded iron formations largely ceased after 1.85 Ga.
Gunflint microfossils show photosynthesis in an atmosphere with enough oxygen for microbial life.

statherian-period.text: The last Paleoproterozoic period, 1800–1600 Ma, is named from the Greek for stable: on most continents new platforms formed or fold belts became cratons.
Columbia had assembled by the start of the period.
Columbia kept growing along its margins through subduction-related magmatism and terrane accretion.
Oxygen stood at 10–20% of today's level.
Fossils from North China's Changcheng Group show eukaryotes were already diverse.
Natural nuclear fission reactors ran at Oklo, Gabon, about 1.7 Ga.

mesoproterozoic-era.text: The Mesoproterozoic Era ran from 1,600 to 1,000 Ma and is divided into the Calymmian, Ectasian and Stenian periods.
The supercontinent Columbia broke up between 1500 and 1350 Ma; its fragments regathered as Rodinia around 1100–900 Ma.
Life in this era was once thought purely microbial, but multicellular organisms did exist.
Equatorial temperatures may have been 22–27 °C and the global average about 19 °C, some 4 °C warmer than today.
Ocean water was about 27 °C, while atmospheric oxygen may have stayed below 0.1–1% of modern levels.
Old cratons such as the Yilgarn and the Baltic Shield had already been worn down into flattish, subdued terrain.

calymmian-period.text: The Calymmian, first period of the Mesoproterozoic, lasted from 1600 to 1400 Ma; its name means 'cover'.
Sedimentary platform covers spread and expanded over the continents.
Oxygen rose transiently to about 4% of present levels at times between 1.59 and 1.36 Ga.
Some of the first algae, such as Tuanshanzia, and possible fungi lived in North China seas about 1,589 Ma.
The exceptionally preserved microbes of the Volyn biota date to about 1500 Ma.

ectasian-period.text: The Ectasian, meaning 'extension', ran from 1400 to 1200 Ma, the second Mesoproterozoic period.
A day lasted about 17 hours 32 minutes early in the period and 18 hours 28 minutes by its end.
The seafloor was about 50–80% oxidized at the start, a share that declined afterwards.
Columbia stayed intact until at least 1.35 Ga, then fully broke apart around 1.3–1.2 Ga amid dyke swarms.
Rodinia began to assemble in the Ectasian.
Acritarchs continued to appear, alongside a moderate number of other eukaryotes.
Stromatolite colonies and reefs dominated the tidal zones of oceans and seas.

stenian-period.text: The Stenian, last Mesoproterozoic period, ran from 1200 to 1000 Ma; 'narrow' refers to the narrow metamorphic belts left by many orogenies.
Rodinia finished assembling during the Stenian.
Most of the Grenville orogeny took place in this period.
Oxygen was still low, about 0.5–5% of present atmospheric levels.
The Keweenawan Rift, the deepest failed rift on Earth, formed around 1100 Ma.
The red alga Bangiomorpha, the oldest known sexually reproducing organism, appeared around 1.047 Ga.
Stromatolites peaked and then declined swiftly around 1 Ga, while eukaryotes came to dominate non-marine habitats.

neoproterozoic-era.text: The Neoproterozoic, last era of the Proterozoic, spans 1000 to 538.8 Ma and holds the Tonian, Cryogenian and Ediacaran periods.
At its start the supercontinent Rodinia, holding most of Earth's land, straddled the equator.
A second surge of oxygen, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event, drove rapid evolution of multicellular life late in the era.
Marine algae proliferated widely, feeding the seafloor and spurring the evolution of microbial eukaryotic predators.
Complex life appears: the primitive sponge Otavia in the Tonian, then the Ediacaran biota with the oldest definite cnidarians and bilaterians.

tonian-period.text: The Tonian ran from 1000 to about 720 Ma; its name, 'stretch', recalls continental crust stretching as Rodinia broke up.
Rodinia and the Mirovian superocean stayed stable through the early Tonian; Rodinia reached its greatest extent around 900 Ma.
Atmospheric oxygen rose to over 13% of present levels between 900 and 815 Ma.
Carbon isotope values climbed from Mesoproterozoic levels to high values late in the period, with deep excursions after 740 Ma.
Acritarchs underwent their first large evolutionary radiation.
Early multicellular organisms may have diversified in deep-ocean oxygen oases, but widespread anoxia kept eukaryotic diversity low.
Molecular studies place the base of the animal family tree in the Tonian.

cryogenian-period.text: The Cryogenian, from 720 to 635 Ma, was a time of drastic climate change; its name means 'cold-making'.
Rodinia was rifting apart, and the proto-Pacific Panthalassa grew by subduction as the superocean Mirovia closed.
The continents all sat at tropical latitudes, so rock weathering kept drawing down carbon dioxide even as Earth cooled.
Two worldwide glaciations, the Sturtian and Marinoan, were the most severe ice ages in Earth's history, with glaciers reaching sea level near the equator.
Average surface temperature was about 5 °C, with carbon dioxide near 1300 ppm and oxygen about 12% of the air.
Between the glaciations came a warmer interval with anoxic oceans and rising seas.
Global biodiversity was very low, though testate amoebae appeared and single-celled algae multiplied a hundred- to thousand-fold.
Some researchers argue the oldest sponge fossils, and so the first animals, date from this period.

ediacaran-period.text: The Ediacaran, from 635 to 538.8 Ma, is the last period of the Proterozoic, named after South Australia's Ediacara Hills.
As Rodinia broke up, Gondwana began assembling through the Pan-African, East African and Kuungan orogenies.
By the end of the Proterozoic most continental mass lay united around the south pole.
It opened as the Cryogenian snowball ended and saw the first widespread complex multicellular life.
Oxygen rose, though the deep ocean stayed anoxic until about 580 Ma and anoxic episodes recurred.
Microbial mats carpeted the sea floor, and Ediacaran fossils are almost always found in mat-bearing beds.
The Ediacaran biota resembled segmented worms, fronds, discs or immobile bags; hard-shelled animals appeared only at the very end.
Seas favoured aragonite and high-magnesium carbonate, and phosphorus levels were well below those of later oceans.

cambrian-period.text: The Cambrian lasted 51.95 million years, from 538.8 to 486.85 Ma, and is the first period of the Paleozoic.
As Gondwana rotated anticlockwise, the south pole moved from off western South America to northwest Africa by the mid-Cambrian.
Laurentia straddled the equator, bordered by the Panthalassa, Iapetus and Khanty oceans; wide oceans separated all the major continents.
The climate was warm and mild, with most continental crust near the equator; models give global averages of about 20–25 °C.
Sea level rose gradually through the period, flooding continental interiors with shallow seas.
Ocean chemistry swung often: at least ten carbon isotope excursions are recognised, more than later in the Phanerozoic.
Land had no plants; microbial mats and biofilms covered tidal flats and beaches and helped form early soils.
Life was in the sea, and unusual preservation makes Cambrian soft-tissue Lagerstätten unusually abundant.

terreneuvian-epoch.text: The Terreneuvian, the first Cambrian epoch, ran from 538.8 to about 521 Ma and holds the Fortunian and the unnamed Stage 2.
Its base is the first Treptichnus pedum burrow; its top is the first appearance of trilobites.
It is the only Cambrian series with no trilobite fossils.
Global average temperatures were about 20–22 °C, cooler than the rest of the Cambrian.
The second phase of the Cambrian explosion played out, yet deuterostomes were absent apart from the possible Yanjiahella.
Avalonia, Ganderia and other peri-Gondwanan terranes lay in polar regions, while North China sat at equatorial to tropical latitudes.

cambrian-series-2-epoch.text: Series 2 lasted from about 521 to 506.5 Ma and is split into the unnamed Stages 3 and 4.
Its base has no GSSP yet; it is expected to be the first appearance of trilobites in Gondwana.
Animals diversified rapidly, but trilobites and archaeocyaths were regionally restricted, making global correlation hard.
About 514 Ma, Laurentia lay on the equator, Siberia just south of it, and Gondwana mostly in the Southern Hemisphere.
Archaeocyath reefs diversified rapidly in Stage 3, then declined sharply in Stage 4.
Nektaspid arthropods were most diverse in this epoch.

miaolingian-epoch.text: The Miaolingian, roughly the old middle Cambrian, lasted from about 506.5 to 497 Ma and holds the Wuliuan, Drumian and Guzhangian.
Laurentia drifted south and rotated about 20° anticlockwise, before drifting north again in the late Cambrian.
Mountain building on Gondwana's Australian–Antarctic margin increased weathering and nutrient supply, raising ocean productivity.
Peri-Gondwanan terranes such as Avalonia had moved to high-to-mid southern latitudes.
Most modern mollusc groups, including gastropods, bivalves, cephalopods and monoplacophorans, were present.
Benthic graptolites became widespread on the sea floor.
Paradoxides, large to very large trilobites, lived worldwide.

furongian-epoch.text: The Furongian, the last Cambrian epoch, ran from about 497 to 486.85 Ma, with the Paibian, Jiangshanian and unnamed Stage 10.
Gondwana stretched from the south pole in northwest Africa to subtropical latitudes, with East Antarctica near the equator.
Trilobite provinces show only a moderate pole-to-equator temperature gradient.
Sea level fluctuated with ice-cap melt from the late Cambrian through the Ordovician.
Subduction began along Gondwana's proto-Andean margin and on northern North China, where the Bainaimiao arc developed.
Trilobites reached their greatest diversity and dominated nearly all fossil assemblages; green algae were common.
Seawater 87Sr/86Sr fell sharply late in the epoch as Gondwana's mountains were worn down and weathering slowed.

ordovician-period.text: Gondwana, holding the southern continents, stretched from north of the equator to the South Pole.
Laurentia, Siberia and Baltica were separate continents, and the Panthalassic Ocean covered much of the Northern Hemisphere.
Most continents lay near the equator, and very high sea levels spread shallow seas across North America, Europe and Gondwana.
Sea level stood about 180 m above today's, rising to 220 m before falling sharply in the end-Ordovician glaciations.
The climate moved from an early greenhouse to icehouse conditions in the Hirnantian, and atmospheric oxygen rose.
The Sun was fainter: 450 million years ago Earth received about 1,312 W per square metre, against about 1,361 today.
Life was dominated by marine animals: trilobites, brachiopods, nautiloids, graptolites, corals and echinoderms filled the seas.
Green algae were common, and the first land plants were simple forms similar to mosses and liverworts.

early-ordovician-epoch.text: The Iapetus Ocean between Gondwana, Laurentia and Baltica was over 4,000 km wide.
The South Pole lay in what is now northern Africa, and Baltica sat near Gondwana in southern latitudes.
Laurentia lay in the southern tropics; today's central Nevada and western Utah were under the sea.
The climate was a hot greenhouse, with sea surface temperatures like those of the Early Eocene, and very high CO2.
Sea level rose more or less continuously, flooding continental shelves.
Trilobites shared the seas with new corals, brachiopods, bryozoans, planktonic graptolites, conodonts and the first true starfish.

middle-ordovician-epoch.text: The climate cooled to a more temperate state; by the epoch's end low-latitude seas matched today's equatorial temperatures.
Trilobite-dominated shelves gave way to mixed communities of brachiopods, bryozoans, molluscs and echinoderms.
Marine animals dispersed widely across narrowing oceans such as the Iapetus.
Acritarchs, mostly marine algae, peaked in diversity.
Labechiid stromatoporoids spread worldwide, building reefs from South China to eastern North America.
Baltica already had a diverse flora of early land plants by the Darriwilian.
After an asteroid broke up in space, meteorites fell on Earth far more often than today.

late-ordovician-epoch.text: Gondwana lay over the South Pole, and the centre of glaciation sat in what is now the Sahara.
Tropical oceans were about 5 °C cooler than today.
Avalonia slowed as it neared Baltica and collided with it; brachiopods and trilobites could now spread between converging continents.
Sea level kept rising at the start of the epoch, then fell for about 3 million years before the Hirnantian glaciation.
The Kazakh terranes formed an archipelago of island arcs and microcontinents on the Equator, and the Proto-Tethys Ocean reached its widest.
Armoured jawless fish such as Arandaspis swam the seas, and the first jawed vertebrates may have appeared.
Planktonic graptolites thrived, and volcanic ash beds are common in rocks of this age.

silurian-period.text: Gondwana covered the equator and much of the southern hemisphere, while the vast Panthalassa Ocean filled most of the northern hemisphere.
Gondwana kept drifting slowly toward high southern latitudes; the South Pole moved from northern Africa to west of southern Chile.
Smaller oceans included the Proto- and Paleo-Tethys, the Rheic, the narrowing Iapetus and the newly formed Ural Ocean.
Earth was in a warm greenhouse state, with CO2 around 4,500 ppm and warm shallow seas over much of the equatorial land.
High seas over flat land made many island chains; sea level rose through the first half of the period and fell through the second.
Far from stable, the climate swung often: the Silurian has more isotope excursions than any other period.
Warm seas fed violent storms that left beds of broken shells.
Life was still mainly marine, though land life was more prominent than ever; the period was partly a long recovery from the end-Ordovician extinction.

llandovery-epoch.text: The Llandovery, or Early Silurian, ran from 443.1 to 432.9 million years ago.
It opened just after the Ordovician–Silurian extinctions, which had sharply cut biodiversity and opened up ecosystems.
Melting ice raised sea level, and after the glacial end of the Ordovician the Rhuddanian climate was much warmer.
Glaciers retreated toward the South Pole early in the Silurian.
Faunas became some of the most cosmopolitan of the Phanerozoic, a pattern that lasted through most of the Silurian.
Widespread reef building began; tentaculitoids radiated in Baltoscandia and camerate crinoids diversified.
Black graptolite shales show oxygen-poor seafloors lasting into the earliest Rhuddanian.
The epoch ended with the Ireviken event, which killed half of trilobite species and 80% of conodont species.

wenlock-epoch.text: Radiometric dates place the Wenlock between 432.9 and 426.7 million years ago; it has two stages, the Sheinwoodian and the Homerian.
The oldest known vascular plants, Cooksonia, appear in the Wenlock.
Air-breathing millipedes from Scotland have been placed in the Wenlock, though their age is disputed.
Laurentia stopped being an independent continent in the middle Silurian as Baltica closed in.
Glaciers had almost vanished by mid-Silurian, yet glacial phases still came from the late Telychian to mid-Sheinwoodian and through the Homerian.
Wenlock limestones of Britain are rich in brachiopods, corals and trilobites such as Calymene.
Eugaleaspid jawless fish diversified, and osteostracans appear, probably in central Euramerica.

ludlow-epoch.text: The Ludlow, or Mid–Late Silurian, ran from 426.7 to 422.7 million years ago, after the Homerian.
The Aymestry Limestone formed in a warm shallow sea near the eastern edge of the Iapetus Ocean.
Scotland–Greenland met Norway around 425 Ma, closing the Iapetus in the Scandian orogeny.
The Ludfordian brought the last major glaciation of the Early Palaeozoic Ice Age and a large fall in sea level.
Lycophytes and zosterophylls joined Cooksonia on land.
Millipedes lived at Kerrera, Scotland, about 425 Ma.
Acanthodians rose in diversity in the Late Silurian, and placoderms such as Silurolepis lived in what is now Yunnan.

pridoli-epoch.text: The Přídolí, the last Silurian epoch, lasted from 422.7 to 419.62 million years ago and was followed by the Lochkovian, first age of the Devonian.
It is named after a locality near Slivenec, a suburb of Prague.
The late Silurian climate was warm and arid, and evaporites filled shallow basins from Michigan to West Virginia.
Warming in the Pridoli ended the Andean-Saharan glaciation and let land plants spread further.
Oxygen rose high enough for the first wildfires, which left the oldest charcoal.
Trilobite diversity dropped sharply and stromatoporoid sponges suffered a second round of extinction.
Scyphocrinoid loboliths appeared suddenly in the terminal Silurian and vanished just as abruptly.

devonian-period.text: The Devonian spans 419.62 to 358.86 Ma, about 60.7 million years, from the end of the Silurian to the start of the Carboniferous.
Laurussia (Euramerica) lay mostly south of the equator and drifted north, while Gondwana covered much of the Southern Hemisphere.
The South Pole lay within Gondwana, moving back to central Africa during the Devonian.
The Rheic Ocean, wide at the start, separated Laurussia from Gondwana; Siberia began the period upside down relative to today.
Sea levels were generally high and fell gradually through the period.
It was a relatively warm period, probably without glaciers for most of it, though climate varied greatly between epochs and regions.
Trilobites, brachiopods and great reefs were still common, and fishes diversified so much that it is called the 'Age of Fishes'.
Silurian moss forests and microbial mats were joined by rooted plants, and by the period's end by trees up to 30 m tall.

early-devonian-epoch.text: The Early Devonian lasted from 419.62 to 393.47 Ma and comprises the Lochkovian, Pragian and Emsian stages.
Arid conditions prevailed in Siberia, Australia, North America and China, while Africa and South America had a warm temperate climate.
Tropical sea surfaces averaged about 30 °C, judging from conodont apatite.
Atmospheric oxygen was relatively low, possibly about half of modern values.
Low sea levels split Laurussia's seafloor fauna into separate provinces.
Lichens such as Spongiophyton were unusually prominent on land just before forests developed.
Armoured jawless fishes, thelodonts and petalichthyid placoderms reached their peak diversity.

middle-devonian-epoch.text: The Middle Devonian ran from 393.47 to 382.31 Ma: the Eifelian, then from 387.95 Ma the Givetian.
Laurentia lay in the Southern Hemisphere between the equator and 30°S.
New forests drew carbon from the air and buried it, perhaps cooling the climate by around 5 °C.
Shrub-like forests of lycophytes, horsetails, ferns and progymnosperms spread, and the earliest trees appeared.
Armoured jawless fishes declined while jawed fishes thrived in both oceans and fresh water.
Stromatoporoid reef sponges reached their greatest diversity in the Eifelian.
Shallow, warm, oxygen-poor inland lakes ringed by early plants favoured fishes with lungs that could crawl briefly onto land.

late-devonian-epoch.text: The Late Devonian began with the Frasnian (382.31-372.15 Ma), when the first forests took shape, followed by the Famennian until 358.86 Ma.
Gondwana covered much of the Southern Hemisphere, and much of South America lay under shallow seas.
Climate warmed back to Early Devonian levels, and temperate climates became more common than arid ones.
Extensive oxidized sediments in Euramerica record severe droughts.
Plants and insects had colonized the land, and Archaeopteris forests spread rapidly.
Lycophytes became a dominant part of the flora.
Rifting and mantle plumes brought flood basalts to Siberia.
Temperatures began to drop late in the epoch, with a short-lived glaciation in the late Famennian.

carboniferous-period.text: The Carboniferous lasted about 60 million years, from 358.86 to 298.9 Ma; its name, from the Latin for coal, marks the coal beds laid down worldwide.
Gondwana covered the south polar region with Laurussia to its northwest; the continents ringed the opening Paleo-Tethys Ocean, with vast Panthalassa beyond.
Plate motions quickened as Gondwana and Laurussia fused into the supercontinent Pangaea.
The climate was dominated by the Late Paleozoic Ice Age, the longest and most extensive icehouse of the Phanerozoic.
Atmospheric oxygen rose from 15–20% at the start of the period to highs of 25–30%.
Towering lycopsid rainforests dominated the tropical belt of Euramerica, the high point of Paleozoic land plants.
Sometimes called the Age of Amphibians, it saw temnospondyls become the dominant land vertebrates and the first amniotes appear.
Air-breathing insects, myriapods and arachnids lived on land, some at giant sizes; at sea, crinoids, sharks and ray-finned fish flourished.

mississippian-subperiod.text: The Mississippian, the earlier of the two Carboniferous subperiods, lasted from 358.86 to 323.4 Ma.
A sea-level drop at the end of the Devonian reversed early on, spreading shallow epicontinental seas and widespread carbonate deposition.
Sea level then fell from about 120 m above today's level to present-day levels by the subperiod's end.
A seaway through the Rheic Ocean linked the Paleo-Tethys and Panthalassa, so marine animals spread almost worldwide.
South America lay at south polar latitudes as Gondwana's westernmost part; the South Pole sat in southern Africa.
The Early Tournaisian Warm Interval had a global average temperature near 22 °C, before short glaciations returned.
Early forests were sparse and coal scarce, though some trees reached 40 m; shallow seas covered much of Siberia.
Crinoids carpeted the sea floor, and sharks and ray-finned fish took over the oceans after the end-Devonian crisis.

pennsylvanian-subperiod.text: The Pennsylvanian, the later Carboniferous subperiod, lasted from 323.4 to 298.9 Ma.
Laurussia straddled the Equator, covered in coal forests; peat mires filled basins beside the Central Pangean Mountains and fringed the China cratons.
Gondwana's ice sheets waxed and waned, swinging sea level and laying cyclothems in shallow tropical seas.
Rheic closure, Pangaea's formation and glaciation confined many marine animals to particular regions.
Oxygen rose above 25% before falling again toward the end of the period.
Lepidodendron and Sigillaria trees dominated the swamps, with horsetails and seed ferns between; conifers and cycads grew on drier ground.
Amniotes appeared and split into sauropsids and synapsids; cockroach relatives were the most successful insects.
By the period's end the South Pole had drifted to eastern Antarctica and equatorial Pangaea was drying out.

permian-period.text: The Permian, the last period of the Paleozoic, lasted about 47 million years, from 298.9 to 251.902 Ma; it is named after Russia's Perm region.
Nearly all land formed one supercontinent, Pangaea, reaching from the equator to both poles, with the microcontinents of Cathaysia lying to the east.
Pangaea's vast interior had a continental climate of extreme heat and cold, megamonsoon rains and widespread deserts.
The world swung from icehouse to greenhouse, with global average temperatures rising from about 12° to over 30° by the Permian–Triassic boundary.
Four floral provinces are recognised: Angaran, Euramerican, Gondwanan and Cathaysian.
Synapsids and sauropsids diversified, and synapsids, the ancestors of mammals, dominated the land.
In the seas brachiopods were highly diverse and helped build reefs, while fish diversity stayed relatively low.
Three or possibly four major extinctions struck, ending with the Great Dying, the largest in Earth's history.

cisuralian-epoch.text: The Cisuralian, or Early Permian, ran from 298.9 to 274.4 Ma and is named after the western slopes of the Ural Mountains.
It opened with the Late Paleozoic Ice Age at its peak; glaciers then receded as the climate warmed, drying the continental interiors.
Sea level stood several tens of metres above today's.
Pelycosaurs, diadectids and temnospondyls dominated life on land, and temnospondyls reached their peak diversity.
Insects diversified dramatically, while marine diversity, origination and extinction rates stayed low.
In tropical Cathaysia a wet, frost-free climate kept coal swamps of lycopsids and tree ferns alive, while glossopterid trees spread across southern Gondwana.
North of the Central Pangean Mountains, coal-swamp plants gave way to seasonally dry vegetation in the range's rain shadow.

guadalupian-epoch.text: The Guadalupian, or Middle Permian, is named after the Guadalupe Mountains of New Mexico and Texas; it began 274.4 Ma and ended 259.857 Ma.
It saw the rise of the therapsids, Olson's Extinction and the end-Capitanian mass extinction.
Reefs were abundant worldwide, from Texas to the Zechstein Basin and the Tethys, the high point of Permian reef building.
Equatorial forests had switched to a seasonal wet–dry pattern, with coastal swamps along East Pangaea linking the temperate zones.
Giant dinocephalian therapsids dominated land ecosystems, and Glossopteris floras flourished in Gondwana as glaciation waned.
Sea level fell sharply from the Roadian onward.
Trilobites reached a final peak of diversity.

lopingian-epoch.text: Near the end of the Permian, Pangaea grew drier, a trend driven by the supercontinent's coalescence.
By the end of the Permian, the North China Craton, South China Block and Indochina had fused with each other and with Pangaea.
Continents clustered in the tropics, and a large mountain barrier stood in Pangaea's interior.
Carboniferous-style lycopod and horsetail swamps survived only in Cathaysia, while glossopterid trees dominated southern Gondwana.
Therapsids ruled the land, from sabre-toothed gorgonopsian predators to beaked dicynodont herbivores; dicynodonts and cynodonts may have evolved warm-bloodedness near the period's close.
Insect origination and extinction rates both dropped markedly toward the end of the Permian.
The late Permian was already hard on marine life; Bowen Basin rocks record repeated marine stress in the middle to late Lopingian.

triassic-period.text: Almost all land formed one supercontinent, Pangaea, centred near the equator and covering about a quarter of Earth's surface.
The world ocean, Panthalassa, covered almost 70% of the globe; nearly all its Triassic deep-sea floor has since been subducted.
The climate was mostly hot and dry, with deserts across Pangaea's interior and red sandstones and evaporites as typical deposits.
A greenhouse climate left even the poles ice-free, while the Pangean megamonsoon reached its peak strength.
Sea level stayed low compared with other periods.
Life mixed extinction survivors, short-lived Triassic experiments and newcomers, such as dinosaurs and early mammal relatives, that would shape the Mesozoic.
On land, pseudosuchian and dinosauromorph archosaurs shared dominance, while Dicroidium seed ferns ruled Gondwana's forests.
In the seas, algae with secondary plastids became the most important plankton.

early-triassic-epoch.text: The epoch, 251.902–247 Ma, was the hottest stretch of the Phanerozoic, following the Siberian Traps eruptions.
The poles had a temperate climate, and the flat pole-to-equator temperature gradient may have let tropical species spread poleward.
Life was slowly recovering from the end-Permian extinction; faunas were poor in species and much the same worldwide.
Lystrosaurus was the commonest land vertebrate, and lycopsids such as Pleuromeia dominated sparse floras.
Microbial reefs and mats spread across shallow seas, where ammonoids boomed and crashed.
The first marine reptiles, among them ichthyosaurs, entered the oceans.
In Europe, most Lower Triassic rocks are the continental red beds of the Buntsandstein.

middle-triassic-epoch.text: The Middle Triassic, 247–237 Ma, saw early stages of Pangaea's breakup and the opening of the Tethys Ocean.
It was cooler than the Early Triassic, with temperatures falling through most of the Anisian.
A shallow sea, the Muschelkalk Sea, covered much of central Europe.
Complex ecosystems re-formed 4–6 million years after the extinction, and many groups regained high diversity.
Archosaurs displaced therapsids to become the dominant land vertebrates.
Seed ferns and gymnosperms made up the vegetation; there were still no flowering plants.
Ichthyosaurs, nothosaurs, pachypleurosaurs, placodonts and other marine reptiles thrived, especially around the Tethys.

late-triassic-epoch.text: The Late Triassic opened with the Carnian pluvial episode, a long wet spell that turned the arid interior into lush alluvial forests.
Pangaea formed an arc reaching almost from pole to pole; East Asian blocks joining it in the Late Triassic gave the supercontinent its greatest land area.
Rift valleys with large lakes opened along the future Central Atlantic, from Florida to Newfoundland and across Morocco and Iberia.
The hothouse climate continued, alternating between cooler and warmer spells through the Norian and a cooler Rhaetian, before an extreme warming ended the period.
Sea level, up to 50 m above today's in the Carnian, fell through the Norian to about 50 m below present in the mid-Rhaetian.
Seed-producing gymnosperm forests covered the land, and plant-eaters grew large to digest the tough, nutrient-poor plants.
Crurotarsan archosaurs such as phytosaurs, aetosaurs and rauisuchians ruled the land, filling more niches than the young dinosaurs.
In the seas, neopterygian fishes spread at the expense of ceratitid ammonites, and shastasaurian ichthyosaurs grew to huge sizes.

jurassic-period.text: The Jurassic lasted about 58.3 million years, from 201.4 to 143.1 million years ago, between the Triassic and the Cretaceous.
It was 5–10 °C warmer than today, with roughly four times today's carbon dioxide and no polar ice caps.
Forests grew close to the poles, while deserts and scrubland spread across low latitudes between about 40° north and south.
Both poles lay in open ocean, and the young North Atlantic stayed narrow through the period.
Ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs ruled the seas, and pterosaurs were the dominant flying vertebrates.
Land plants were ferns and gymnosperms: conifers, cycads, ginkgos and the extinct Bennettitales. There were no widely accepted flowering plants.
Sea level rose and fell cyclically, with 64 fluctuations, 15 of them larger than 75 metres.

early-jurassic-epoch.text: The Early Jurassic, 201.4 to 174.7 million years ago, was tropical and much more humid than the Triassic as new seas opened between landmasses.
Pangaea still held all the major landmasses at its start but began splitting into Laurasia and Gondwana.
A cool interval lasted from about 199 to 183 million years ago, ended by a sharp Toarcian warming.
Tropical seas covered parts of Europe, such as England's Jurassic Coast, laying down the marine rocks called the Lias.
Laurasian and Gondwanan faunas differed considerably.
Dinosaurs spread to every continent, while ichthyosaurs reached their peak species diversity in the seas.
In East Asia's mid-latitudes, forests were dominated by the deciduous broad-leaved conifer Podozamites.

middle-jurassic-epoch.text: The Middle Jurassic spanned 174.7 to 161.5 million years ago.
Pangaea was separating into Laurasia and Gondwana: the young Central Atlantic was widening, and seafloor spreading began in the Gulf of Mexico about 165 Ma.
The seas swarmed with ammonites, ichthyosaurs, sharks, rays and ray-finned fish.
On land, dinosaurs flourished in forests of cycads and conifers; conifers were the dominant plants.
Middle Jurassic land-animal fossils are relatively rare; key sites include England's Forest Marble and China's Daohugou Beds.
Sea level rose from the Aalenian onward, and in northeast China the climate was warm, humid and subtropical to temperate.
The Middle Jurassic opened as the Toarcian Warm Interval gave way to the Middle Jurassic Cool Interval, possibly broken by brief ice ages.
In the Callovian the shallow Turgai Sea formed a marine barrier between Europe and Asia.
Europe turned more humid at the start of the Bajocian, then drier during the middle Bajocian.
Sauropods diversified, and megalosaurids, the oldest radiation of tetanuran predators, appeared in Europe.
Mammals branched out: the first crown-group mammals, early multituberculates, furred Castorocauda and the gliding Volaticotherium.
The first unambiguous squamates, including early lizards, appear in Bathonian rocks of the Northern Hemisphere.
In northeastern China, layers of volcanic tuff buried the Yanliao Biota, with dinosaurs, mammals, salamanders, insects and plants.

late-jurassic-epoch.text: The Late Jurassic spans about 161.5 to 143.1 million years ago.
Pangaea had split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south, divided by the wide Tethys Ocean.
Narrow new ocean basins were opening between East Gondwana, West Gondwana and Laurasia, and a still-narrow Atlantic separated Europe from North America.
Very high carbon dioxide kept the world hot; the Kimmeridgian Warm Interval was among the Jurassic's wettest times, though Europe grew more arid.
Europe was an archipelago in a shallow, warm tropical sea at the edge of the Tethys, much nearer the equator than today.
Sponge and coral reefs spread widely, and a carbonate platform nearly 7,000 km long fringed eastern North America.
In western North America, rivers built the Morrison floodplains, home to giant sauropods such as Apatosaurus, Brachiosaurus and Diplodocus alongside Allosaurus.
Small predatory theropods gave rise to the first birds such as Archaeopteryx, while pterosaurs neared their greatest diversity.

cretaceous-period.text: The Cretaceous ran from about 143.1 to 66 Ma and is named for its chalk; more chalk formed then than in any other Phanerozoic period.
Pangaea finished breaking into today's continents, though they sat in different places; North America was cut off from the rest.
The climate was hot and humid, with lush forests at the poles, no permanent ice and seas around 300 metres higher than today.
At the peak of the Cretaceous flooding, a third of today's land lay under shallow, warm seas that laid down limestone.
Pollen records show three broad climate phases: warm and dry (Berriasian–Barremian), warm and wet (Aptian–Santonian), then cool and dry (Campanian–Maastrichtian).
Coccolithophore algae thrived in the seas, and rudist bivalves built the reefs of the Tethys.
The Alps did not yet exist; Europe's southern continental shelf faced the Tethys Ocean.
Many of today's dominant groups trace their origins to the Cretaceous, as flowering plants spread and insects diversified.

early-cretaceous-epoch.text: The Early Cretaceous spans 143.1 to 100.5 Ma.
The cooling of the latest Jurassic carried into the Berriasian, with common snowfall at high latitudes and wetter tropics than before.
Gondwana began the period whole; South America, Antarctica and Australia then rifted from Africa, opening the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
Seaways expanded while sauropods, stegosaurs and other high-browsing plant-eaters declined.
Archaic mammals such as eutriconodonts were common, and dinosaurs became distinct from one landmass to the next.
Forests were dominated by conifers such as podocarps, pines, araucarias and cypresses, with ginkgos, bennettitaleans and ferns.
The inland Eromanga Sea covered much of Australia, while a proto-Amazon–Congo river flowed west across western Gondwana.
By the late Albian, tropical seas averaged about 30 °C.

late-cretaceous-epoch.text: The Late Cretaceous spans 100.5 to 66 Ma.
It stayed warmer than today but cooled over time, a trend that continued into the Cenozoic; the tropics shrank toward the equator and northern seasons sharpened.
The Western Interior Seaway joined the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean, splitting North America into Laramidia in the west and Appalachia in the east.
Hadrosaurs, ankylosaurs and ceratopsians thrived in Asiamerica, western North America plus eastern Asia, and tyrannosaurs were North America's top predators.
Flowering plants grew ever more diverse, though in many places ferns and conifers were still more common.
Tethys seas held marine reptiles, bony and cartilaginous fish and cephalopods; mosasaurs appeared and, once the ichthyosaurs vanished, ruled the seas while plesiosaurs persisted.
The Arctic was warm enough for choristodere reptiles to colonise it.
The Americas drifted west and the Atlantic widened; India headed north toward Asia, and Europe was a chain of islands.
Australia and Antarctica stayed joined and began drifting away from Africa and South America, while a shallow sea at times cut Africa in two.
The epoch opened in one of the Phanerozoic's hottest spells, with the highest carbon dioxide of the Cretaceous.
Near its end, Antarctica still had a tropical to subtropical climate, temperate rainforest and marsupials.

paleogene-period.text: The Paleogene, first period of the Cenozoic, spans about 43 million years, from the end of the Cretaceous at 66 Ma to the Neogene at 23.04 Ma.
It begins with the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs and is divided into the Paleocene, Eocene and Oligocene epochs.
Its climate swung from the heat of the PETM through Eocene cooling to the first permanent Antarctic ice sheets at the start of the Oligocene.
At its start, the Pacific Ocean floor was made of the Pacific, Farallon, Kula and Izanagi plates.
The last pieces of Gondwana came apart as Antarctica separated from South America and Australia, opening the Drake and Tasmanian Passages.
From the Late Cretaceous into the early Paleocene, Africa began converging on Eurasia.
Mammals reached their modern diversity in the Paleogene and Neogene and have been the dominant land animals since 66 Ma.

paleocene-epoch.text: The Paleocene lasted from 66 to 56 Ma and is divided into the Danian, Selandian and Thanetian ages.
Earth was a greenhouse world averaging about 24–25 °C, against about 14 °C in recent times, with no permanent ice at the poles.
The deep ocean was 8–12 °C, compared with 0–3 °C today, and sinking water formed in the North Pacific rather than the North Atlantic.
Northern continents were still joined by land bridges, while South America, Antarctica and Australia had not fully separated.
The Rockies were rising, the Americas were not yet joined, India had begun colliding with Asia, and the North Atlantic Igneous Province was forming.
Forests grew worldwide, even at the poles; they were dense for lack of large plant-eaters but poor in plant species. Australia was warm, wet and rainforested.
Mostly small, fast-evolving animals filled the emptied world; the largest land carnivores were reptiles such as crocodyliforms, choristoderes and snakes.
In the seas, ray-finned fish rose to dominate the open ocean and recovering reefs.

eocene-epoch.text: Through the Eocene the continents kept drifting toward their present positions; early on, Australia and South America were still joined to Antarctica.
Around 50 million years ago Eurasia was split into Western Europe, Balkanatolia and Asia, while South America stayed linked to an ice-free Antarctica.
Earth averaged about 27 °C at the start of the Eocene, and greenhouse gases, chiefly carbon dioxide and methane, controlled surface temperatures.
Climate warmed from the PETM to a peak around 49 million years ago, then cooled through the rest of the epoch until ice sheets appeared on Antarctica.
Eocene oceans were warm and teeming with fish, and plants and sea life took on a quite modern look.
Early Eocene mammals were mostly small, living in cramped jungles; members of the new orders weighed under 10 kg.
In western North America, huge lakes filled the high, flat basins between rising mountains.
By the epoch's end, continental interiors were drying, forests had thinned and open, arid habitats were spreading.

oligocene-epoch.text: The Oligocene links the archaic, tropical world of the Eocene with the more modern ecosystems of the Miocene.
Its base is fixed at Massignano, near Ancona in Italy, at the last appearance of the foraminifer Hantkenina.
The continents kept drifting toward their present positions, and Antarctica grew more isolated as deep ocean channels opened toward Australia and South America.
Sea levels were lower than in the early Eocene, exposing wide coastal plains in Europe and along North America's Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
The epoch opened with a massive spread of Antarctic ice, and both poles fell well below freezing for the first time in the Phanerozoic.
Climate cooled overall after the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum; land temperatures in North America fell 7–11 °C in the earliest Oligocene.
Open plains and grasses spread as forests retreated, and land and sea life reached a Phanerozoic low in diversity by the late Oligocene.
Isolated South America and Australia kept their own native animals; in South America, terror birds and carnivorous marsupial relatives remained top predators.

neogene-period.text: Through the Neogene the continents sat very close to their present positions.
India kept pushing into Asia, raising the Himalayas.
Late in the period the Isthmus of Panama formed, joining North and South America.
Global climate cooled markedly through the Neogene, leading into the continental glaciations of the Quaternary.
Mammals and birds remained the dominant land animals, spreading into many habitats.
Huge predators such as megalodon and the sperm whale Livyatan ruled the oceans.
The first humans, Homo habilis, appeared in Africa near the end of the period.

miocene-epoch.text: The long cooling was broken by relatively short warmer spells; in one, the global climate rivalled the Oligocene's.
In the Early Miocene, temperature differences between mid-latitude lands and seas were much like today's.
Grasslands kept spreading and forests kept shrinking, as in the Oligocene.
Plants and animals were recognisably modern, and many of today's mammal groups first appeared.
Far northern Australia had monsoons, and central Australia held rainforest pockets that a drier climate later shrank.

late-miocene.text: The Late Miocene, made up of the Tortonian and Messinian stages, lasted from 11.63 to 5.333 Ma.
About 11 Ma the warm Middle Miocene gave way to the cooler Late Miocene, and the climate grew increasingly like today's.
Of today's major geographic features only a land bridge between the Americas was missing, though islands began forming between them.
The Andes kept rising, lifting the future Altiplano from low ground to over 3,000 m.
Cut off from the oceans, the Paratethys had become a vast brackish megalake reaching from the eastern Alps to Kazakhstan.
Grasslands and savannas were established by about 10 Ma; global cooling dried the world, especially after 8–7 Ma, and C4 grasses became significant 7–6 Ma.
Recognisable canids, bears, deer, camels and whales lived alongside now-extinct three-toed horses, gomphotheres and hornless rhinos.
Late in the epoch the Mediterranean was cut off from the Atlantic and almost completely evaporated.

pliocene-epoch.text: Through the Pliocene the continents kept drifting toward their present positions, ending up within about 70 km of where they are today.
The climate grew cooler, drier and more seasonal, a bridge between the warm Miocene and the icy Pleistocene.
Cooling may have thinned forests and spread grasslands and savannas; Central Asia became more seasonal and C4 plants grew more common.
The oceans stayed fairly warm though slowly cooling, and Pliocene seas were full of sea cows, seals, sea lions, sharks and whales.
Wet 'Green Sahara' phases returned to North Africa about every 21,000 years, strongest when Earth's orbit was most eccentric.
Hoofed animals dominated Africa, where australopithecines and baboon-like monkeys such as Dinopithecus appeared.
Elephants, gomphotheres and stegodonts thrived in Asia; the largest land mammals were proboscideans such as Deinotherium, Anancus and Mammut borsoni.
In Australia, meat-eating marsupials still hunted, including dasyurids, the dog-like thylacine and the cat-like Thylacoleo.

quaternary-period.text: The Pleistocene lasted from about 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago, spanning the world's most recent period of repeated glaciations.
It is the first epoch of the Quaternary, the shortest geological period of the Phanerozoic.
Since 2009 its start has been set at 2.58 Ma, so that all the recent repeated glaciations fall within it.
Perhaps as many as 44 glacial–interglacial cycles have passed since it began, while the Antarctic ice sheet has persisted throughout.

pleistocene-epoch.text: The Pleistocene lasted from about 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago, spanning the world's most recent period of repeated glaciations.
It is the first epoch of the Quaternary, the shortest geological period of the Phanerozoic.
Since 2009 its start has been set at 2.58 Ma, so that all the recent repeated glaciations fall within it.
Perhaps as many as 44 glacial–interglacial cycles have passed since it began, while the Antarctic ice sheet has persisted throughout.
Its first part, the Early Pleistocene (2.58–0.774 Ma), comprises the Gelasian and Calabrian ages.
In the Early Pleistocene archaic Homo arose in Africa and spread across Afro-Eurasia; Homo erectus was the only hominin for much of the epoch.
Great Britain was then a peninsula of Europe, joined by a chalk ridge across the Strait of Dover, and the Rhine flowed through today's North Sea.
In North America, the early and middle Pleistocene glacials and interglacials, about 2.5–0.2 Ma, are grouped as the Pre-Illinoian.

gelasian-age.text: The Gelasian spans 2.58–1.80 Ma, following the Pliocene's Piacenzian Age and preceding the Calabrian.
It was moved from the Pliocene to the Pleistocene in 2009 to match key changes in Earth's climate, oceans and life at 2.58 Ma.
Its base is the Gauss–Matuyama reversal, marked at Monte San Nicola in Sicily; its top is the end of the Olduvai subchron.
Northern Hemisphere ice sheets began to grow; deep-sea cores record about 40 marine isotope stages, MIS 103 to 64, within the age.
In the Alps the Gelasian corresponds to the Biber glacial complex, with about 20 glacial cycles of varying intensity.
In East Anglia the Red, Norwich and Weybourne Crag formations were laid down, recording early Pleistocene environments.

calabrian-age.text: The Calabrian runs from 1.80 Ma to 774,000 years ago, about a million years, as the second age of the Early Pleistocene.
Its base lies just above the Olduvai subchron at Vrica in Calabria, Italy; it ends with the Brunhes–Matuyama reversal.
Glacial cycles were paced mainly by the 41,000-year obliquity cycle, until the Mid-Pleistocene Transition near the end of the age.
In the Alps the Danube glacial stage, about 1.8–1 Ma, falls within the Calabrian.
The ICS chart places the Waalian interglacial of northern Europe at about 1.6–1.4 Ma.
Homo erectus colonised Eurasia between about 1.8 and 0.8 Ma.
The oldest ice known in Greenland is about 1 million years old.

chibanian-age.text: The Chibanian, or Middle Pleistocene, runs from the Brunhes–Matuyama magnetic reversal to roughly the end of the Penultimate Glacial Period.
The continents sat essentially where they are now, having moved no more than about 100 km since the Pleistocene began.
Glacial cycles now came about every 100,000 years: long glacial periods broken by short, warm interglacials.
At peak glaciation sea level fell by up to 120 m, exposing continental shelves as dry land and linking landmasses.
Ice sheets 1,500–3,000 m thick spread over North America and northern Europe, pushing to the 40th parallel in places.
Faunas were essentially modern but rich in large mammals such as mammoths, mastodons, sabre-toothed cats, giant sloths and Gigantopithecus.
Archaic humans such as Homo heidelbergensis spread through Africa and Eurasia, and the age closes with Neanderthals, Denisovans and early Homo sapiens.

late-pleistocene-age.text: After the brief, warm Last Interglacial, the Late Pleistocene was dominated by the cool Last Glacial Period, coldest at the Last Glacial Maximum.
Eurasia was mostly cold, with glaciations in northern Europe, northwest Siberia and the Alps between temperate interglacial phases.
At its height the Laurentide ice sheet reached from the Rockies through the Great Lakes into New England, covering nearly all of Canada.
A vast mammoth steppe stretched from Spain across Eurasia and Beringia into Alaska and the Yukon.
As the epoch began, proboscideans numbered about 23 species, and over 30 species of ground sloths lived across the Americas.
In Africa, glacial cycles and sea-level swings shaped vertebrate communities more than tectonics or volcanoes did.
Lakes swelled in closed basins of the Great Basin, such as Lake Lahontan, and in the high Andes.
Modern humans spread across the ice-free world, interbreeding with archaic humans they met outside Africa.
Around 18,000 years ago, near the end of the Last Glacial Maximum, global sea level stood 120–130 m below today's.
Low seas joined Maui, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi into one island and linked Mayor Island to the rest of New Zealand.
Ice blocked the Beringia land bridge around 18,000 BP, and massive ice sheets covered most of Canada and the northwest coast.
From about 16,000 years ago until the Pleistocene's end, climate swung between cold stadials and warmer interstadials.
Global mean annual temperature rose about 6 °C between 15,000 and 10,000 years ago.
By around 13,000 years ago sea level was only 60 m below present; on the Great Barrier Reef's coastal plain, corals began ringing hills turned into islands.
Around 12,000 BCE, Great Britain, much of the North Sea and the English Channel formed one expanse of low-lying tundra.
The mammoth steppe, which had covered much of the north for about 100,000 years, shrank to small patches around 12,000 years ago.

holocene-epoch.text: The Holocene, the current epoch, began about 11,700 years ago, at the end of the Younger Dryas cold spell; its GSSP lies in Greenland's NGRIP2 ice core.
It is an interglacial within the ongoing Quaternary glacial cycles, equivalent to Marine Isotope Stage 1.
Continents moved less than a kilometre over 10,000 years, so the map was essentially today's.
Melting ice raised world sea level about 35 m in the early Holocene and another 30 m later, while land once under glaciers rebounded as much as 180 m.
In 2018 the epoch was split by climate into three ages: Greenlandian, Northgrippian and Meghalayan.
Its ecosystems kept losing species after the Late Pleistocene die-off of most large land mammals outside Africa.
It is often called the Age of Humans, spanning farming, the rapid spread of people and all of written history.

greenlandian-age.text: The Greenlandian, the earliest age of the Holocene, runs from about 11,700 to 8,200 years ago and ends with the 8.2-kiloyear cooling event.
After the abrupt warming that ended the ice age, global warming continued at a somewhat gentler pace.
Rising seas drowned vast lowlands, cutting off the British Isles, Indonesia, New Guinea and Tasmania.
The Bering land bridge went under, opening the Bering Strait between Asia and the Americas.
A stronger African monsoon turned much of the Sahara into grassland, woodland and lakes.
Many megafauna species died out, continuing the Late Pleistocene extinctions.
Eurasia entered the Mesolithic, while in the Near East farming and herding began the Neolithic.

northgrippian-age.text: The age opened with the 8.2 ka cold spell; then a warming climate and melting ice raised sea levels, flooding Doggerland and Sundaland.
After the cold spell, temperatures climbed to the Holocene's highest, so the age's first part was the Holocene Climatic Optimum.
Polar ice caps shrank to their smallest extent of the Holocene, and air masses and rain belts shifted from today's pattern.
Six thousand years ago the Sahara was about half today's size, and Lake Mega-Chad once spread over some 350,000 km².
A stronger East African monsoon raised lake levels, while western North America was drier than today.
The El Niño–Southern Oscillation was much weaker than in the later Holocene.
Across much of the world, people moved from foraging to farming and herding, entering the Neolithic.

meghalayan-age.text: The Meghalayan, the latest age of the Holocene, began 4,250 years before 2000 with the 4.2-kiloyear drought and runs to the present day.
It is named after the Indian state of Meghalaya, where a stalagmite in Mawmluh Cave marks its base; it was ratified in June 2018.
After the rapid post-glacial rise, sea level stayed nearly stable from about 4,200 years ago until its rise sped up between 1850 and 1900.
Africa has been relatively cool since 4,000 BP, and Late Holocene cold snaps in East Asia tracked solar minima.
Monsoonal China grew more arid, while north-western Patagonia turned more humid once the Holocene Climatic Optimum ended.
El Niño, weak in the Middle Holocene, strengthened to moderate or high levels over the Late Holocene.
Fire activity in Siberia fell again, and a 1,500-year North Atlantic circulation cycle may have been felt worldwide.
Moa, New Zealand's giant flightless birds, were still thriving in the Late Holocene, before human settlers arrived.
Iceland's eruptions, such as Laki in 1783, come from the North American and Eurasian plates pulling apart at a divergent boundary.
Orbital cycles drove a slow Northern Hemisphere cooling over the last 2,000 years, through the Middle Ages and Little Ice Age, about 0.02 °C per century in the Arctic.
Warmth in the eleventh and early fifteenth centuries gave way to cool seventeenth and early nineteenth centuries; the twentieth century was warmest.
Large eruptions repeatedly chilled the climate, with three big volcanic cooling periods in 1641–1642, 1667–1694 and 1809–1831.
Humans lived on every continent but Antarctica, first sighted in 1820; East Polynesia, including New Zealand, was among the last habitable land settled.
By the Middle Ages, clearing and farming made humans the strongest force shaping Europe's land surface.
Extinctions followed people to islands: Polynesian expansion wiped out many species, and 95% of bird extinctions since the late 15th century were island natives.
By the 2010s the global average temperature was about 15 °C, and year-round ice covered about 3.1% of Earth's surface and 10.7% of its land.
Atmospheric carbon dioxide reached 432 ppm in 2026, 54% above the 280 ppm that held for 10,000 years before the mid-18th century.
Global sea level has risen faster since 1900 than in any century for at least 4,000 years, reaching 4.62 mm a year in 2013–2022.
About 90% of the world's earthquakes, including most of the largest, strike along the Pacific Ring of Fire.
Farming dominates the land: by 2012 about 13% of ice-free land was cropland, 26% pasture and 4% urban or industrial.
Human-made materials now outweigh all of Earth's biomass, and wild mammal biomass has fallen 83% since the dawn of civilization.
Only about 3% of the land surface remains ecologically and faunally intact, with healthy native species and little human footprint.
